newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel says Czech reforms would live without Klaus.
newsitem.headline: Havel says Czech reforms would live without Klaus.

text.p: Czech market reforms would move forward even if their key architect, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, were no longer in charge of the government, President Vaclav Havel said on Friday.
In an interview with Reuters, Havel was asked whether, as some politicians and analysts have suggested, the economy would suffer if Klaus was forced out of office due to recent political turmoil.
"Maybe some people think that but I don't think so," Havel said in Prague Castle.

"I believe that the privatisation processes, the creation of all the instruments of the market economy are so well under way that even if someone wanted to stop them, they don't have a real possiblity to do so."

Havel, a former dissident playwright who has clashed with Klaus over priorities for the transformation of Czech society, is not a member of any political party. He is elected by parliament and is not directly involved in party politics.

Soon after the 1989 revolution which ousted the Communist government, Klaus won acclaim for a rapid voucher-based privatisation scheme that he led, which transferred thousands of companies into private hands.
But the economy, once considered a model of reform, has been hit recently by a huge trade deficit blamed largely on poor corporate restructuring.
That led to fierce speculative attacks on the value of the crown, forcing the central bank to float the currency on May 27, letting it fall even further.
There has been a huge rift in the ruling three-party centre-right coalition, in power since 1992, and the once-popular government's public support has slipped to around 20 percent.
Klaus and top members of his senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS) have said a move to a centre-left government would be a huge blow to investor confidence.
Some analysts have agreed, while others say the reforms are irreversible.
In the interview, Havel praised Klaus for his reforms but said the economy could not depend on one man.
"I have no doubt that Vaclav Klaus deserves much credit for the economic reform of the country, for the speed with which it was pursued and for the achieved successes," Havel said.
"But I don't think we would be a mature democracy if our trade depended on Klaus or Havel or...whoever," he added.
Many Czechs blame Klaus, a confident economics professor, for the economic and political problems. He narrowly survived a confidence vote in parliament last month.
The opposition, led by the centre-left Social Democrats, continue to pressure Klaus to step down but need at least one coalition deputy to cross over to oust him.
Klaus said recently that he considered resigning in late May -- when the coalition negotiated four changes in the 16-member cabinet -- along with his close friend, the finance minister Ivan Kocarnik.
Klaus's centrist coalition partners, the Christian Democrats, continue to battle the two right-wing parties over key issues, threatening a possible collapse of the alliance.
